title: Wanting to go home, leave, or get out of here near death

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source utterance/listening-layer synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe communication patterns and response guidance but do not supply consented verbatim bedside testimony.
This record must not become a prophecy, last-words trope, spiritual proof, diagnosis, countdown, or mandatory script.
Treatment, legal, ritual, emergency, and safety decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: A dying person says they want to go home, leave, or get out, and the witness must hold several possibilities at once: practical location preference, confusion, distress, memory, metaphor, or near-death awareness language.
ordinary_language_queries: dying person wants to go home but already home
take me home at end of life
why does hospice patient say go home
wants to go home before death

content_layers.observation_text: Public and professional sources support treating 'home' language as a cue for listening, not as a single interpretation. The phrase may be literal, relational, spatial, confused, symbolic, or spiritual depending on context.
content_layers.source_synthesis: The seed names 'I want to go home' as a motif. PCNOW frames some end-of-life communication as near-death awareness with symbolic language, and Virtual Hospice treats wanting to go home as a possible cue to ask more rather than assume meaning.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: Utterance records should preserve what was heard, who heard it, and what interpretive frames were available without deciding meaning for the family or turning speech into a rule.

what_this_is_not: not proof that death is imminent
not proof of a spiritual transition
not proof of delirium in every case
not a command to move the person without care-team review
uncertainties: Need consented bedside examples across home, hospital, dementia, and religious/secular contexts.
Public sources do not quantify how often this phrase appears.
Meaning may change sentence by sentence.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should say: this phrase has been heard before, but it does not have one guaranteed meaning. Ask gently what home means right now and involve the care team if there is distress, agitation, or safety concern.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect non-leading follow-up questions, context fields, dementia/delirium boundary notes, and family interpretations without adjudicating them.
language_notes: Prefer 'what might home mean here?' over 'this means they are transitioning.'
Avoid turning one phrase into a clock.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the utterance layer. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, not a legal instruction, not a ritual authority, not proof of spiritual meaning, not a diagnosis of delirium, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical or domain review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent distress, safety, medication, confusion, swallowing, legal, or crisis concerns to qualified local support.
